title: Understanding our model-collapse graphs

pages.title: Understanding our model-collapse graphs
pages.caption: Reading guide to the completed OPT-125M / WikiText-2 experiments. No new training was run for this guide.
pages.subtitle: Graph families, equations, intuition and measured results | 28 October 2026

items.text: Two questions run through the report: can a model still predict genuine text, and what happens to the text it generates? The figures measure both, because the answers can differ.

Behavioural intuition: recursive self-training resembles repeatedly rewriting study notes and learning from the rewrite. Errors and omissions can be copied forward. Continued training keeps earlier weight changes; resetting restores the chosen starting weights, but the rewritten training data still carry the history.
Cycle 0: the real-data-trained reference, called G0 in Week 1 and S0 in Week 2. It is different from untouched pretrained OPT.
Shared beginning: the Week 2 reset/continued arms reuse the exact same S0, S1 and D2. Grey means one shared measurement pair; the arms first differ at cycle 2.
Fair comparisons: Week 1 and continued training have different first-step initializers and used different GPU classes. The shared-start pair matches the beginning and recorded primary environment.
Fixed measurements: all models see the same real validation/test blocks. Output statistics use the first 256 fixed training prompts, each producing exactly 64 new tokens.
Tokens: words, parts of words, punctuation or special symbols. Output statistics use token IDs, including special tokens; a 64-token output is not necessarily 64 words.

How to read the explanations: intuition describes the model's behaviour in everyday terms. 'Likely causes' are interpretations of our results, not established mechanisms. Specific dips and peaks can remain unexplained. Equations and numerical examples show how each measurement is calculated. All logarithms are natural.

pages.title: 1. Real-text loss and perplexity
pages.caption: A/B: fixed real validation and test sets. C: matched test comparison. The shared prefix is reused; the untouched pretrained value 115.43 is omitted from these axes.

items.text: Question: how much probability does the current model assign to the next token actually present in held-out real WikiText? Evaluation supplies the correct real prefix at every position.

Behavioural intuition: the model reads real text and repeatedly encounters the next word. Higher perplexity means it is more surprised by what actually follows: it assigns genuine text less probability and predicts it worse on average. Lower perplexity means the text better matches its expectations.
Equation: x_i is the next token, p_theta the model and N the target count. L averages negative log-probability; PPL = exp(L). Lower is better.
Numerical example: probability 0.1 costs 2.303 nats; 0.01 costs 4.605. PPL 50 corresponds to a geometric mean correct-token probability of 2%, not an accuracy percentage.
Our curves: Week 1 goes 33.88 -> 62.49 -> 52.83. Continued goes 33.89 -> 48.38, recovers to 42.72 at S3, then reaches 55.56. Final reset is 42.10, versus continued 55.56.
Validation versus test: validation chooses checkpoints; held-out test data only report results. Corpus PPL exponentiates mean NLL; it does not average batch perplexities.

Likely cause of the first jump: replacing human targets with selected synthetic continuations shifts the patterns being learned [1]. Week 1 and continued training also use different first-step initializers.

Likely cause of the later separation: resetting to real-trained S0 may limit accumulated weight drift; continued updates may compound the synthetic/real mismatch. This is consistent with the matched curves, but not an isolated mechanism test.

Unresolved dip and plateau: changing synthetic datasets, beam-search choices and real-validation selection could produce partial recovery or a stable biased regime. We have not established why the early dip occurs, or why Week 1 settles at its particular level.

pages.title: 2. Distinct-n: variety of token combinations
pages.caption: A/B show distinct-1/2/3 within each historical condition. C compares distinct-2 after the identical Week 2 beginning. Higher means more unique combinations per occurrence.

items.text: Question: how many different individual tokens, pairs or triples occur in the fixed output sample? An n-gram is n consecutive tokens.

Behavioural intuition: imagine listening to many answers. Does the model use a broad range of building blocks and phrase patterns, or keep reaching for the same ones? Falling distinct-n means fewer different combinations per occurrence; rising values mean more surface variety, not necessarily more knowledge.
Equation: U_n is the number of unique n-gram types and T_n is their total number of occurrences. We form n-grams within each continuation, then pool counts across outputs.
Toy example: A B A B has distinct-1 = 2/4 = 50%; its pairs AB, BA, AB give distinct-2 = 2/3 = 66.7%; its triples ABA, BAB give distinct-3 = 2/2 = 100%.
Read the lines: compare each n with the same n across cycles. Longer sequences have more possible combinations, so distinct-3 naturally tends to exceed distinct-1.
Our results: Week 1 distinct-3 falls 42.83% -> 38.15%, although distinct-2 rises 29.23% -> 30.58%. Continued finishes above S0 on all three ratios; its distinct-2 still falls 19.6% from the S2 peak.
Matched final models: reset distinct-2 is 31.05%, versus continued 34.71%. Reset distinct-3 is 39.02%, versus S0 42.66%. Diversity changes are therefore mixed.

Interpretation limit: these ratios measure token-combination variety, not semantic variety or factual accuracy. Sample sizes are fixed because unique/total ratios depend on output length and sample size.

Likely causes: early fine-tuning changes which continuations beam search prefers, potentially increasing measured variety. Later feedback can reinforce recurring templates and reduce combination variety. That could explain the early peaks and later declines, but it does not uniquely explain the exact peak at cycle 2.

Why the measures disagree: a model can introduce new individual tokens while recombining them in familiar longer phrases. Thus distinct-1/2 can remain above S0 while distinct-3 falls. Similar or even incoherent answers can still contain many different token combinations.

pages.title: 3. Repeated four-token phrases
pages.caption: The same 15,616 within-continuation four-gram positions are counted at every model. Higher values mean more occurrences beyond the first appearance of each four-gram.

items.text: Question: how much of the generated sample reuses four-token combinations that have already appeared?

Behavioural intuition: this detects the model falling back on familiar turns of phrase, such as repeatedly listing the same console or location. A rising curve means more phrase reuse across its answers, even when complete answers are not identical.
Equation: T_4 counts all four-gram occurrences; U_4 counts unique four-gram types. Subtracting unique types leaves the excess occurrences after each first appearance.
Toy example: ten four-gram occurrences containing six unique types give (10 - 6)/10 = 40% repetition.

Scope: a phrase can repeat inside one output or across different outputs. No four-gram crosses an output boundary. Shared Wikipedia-style language can contribute even without a visible looping sentence.
Our results: Week 1 rises 48.87% -> 59.05%; continued rises 48.55% -> 52.36%. The matched reset model finishes at 57.66%, above continued's 52.36%.

Direction: rising repetition can indicate concentrated output, but neither every repeat nor every fluctuation establishes collapse. The initial real-trained model already has substantial phrase reuse.

A 57.66% rate does not mean 57.66% of sentences are identical. This is a four-token occurrence statistic. It equals one minus distinct-4 under the same counting rule; we report distinct-1/2/3 separately.

Likely causes: deterministic beam search favours high-probability sequences and can produce repetitive text [2]. Training on those outputs may then reinforce the same patterns. The later reset arm is consistent with stronger phrase concentration despite its better real-test perplexity.

Why the curve can dip: a change in preferred continuations can temporarily introduce more unique four-grams. The early drop is real, but its precise cause was not isolated. Token reuse need not increase at every cycle.

pages.title: 4. Exact duplicate continuations
pages.caption: Each curve compares 256 complete 64-token outputs generated from the fixed prompt set. Exact equality is tested on token IDs.

items.text: Question: do different prompts lead the model to produce exactly the same complete continuation? This is a stricter comparison than shared phrases.
Equation: subtract the number of unique continuation rows from 256 and divide by 256. The result counts extra copies after the first occurrence.
Toy example: ten outputs with eight unique rows contain two excess copies, so the duplicate rate is 20%. One pair among 256 contributes one extra copy: 1/256 = 0.39%.
Our results: Week 1 ends at 13/256 excess copies (5.08%). Continued ends at 7/256 (2.73%). The shared-start reset model ends at 15/256 (5.86%).

Behavioural intuition: imagine asking several different questions and receiving the same complete answer. More duplicates mean the model is producing fewer distinct full responses across our prompt set, suggesting reduced output variety or prompt sensitivity.

Interpretation limit: near-identical outputs differing by one token count as distinct. This metric can miss heavy repetition inside each output, so it should be read alongside repeated four-grams and examples.

Likely causes: common templates can become preferred for several prompts as synthetic feedback reinforces them. Deterministic decoding repeats the preferred choice; our fixed prompt slice also contains related Wikipedia contexts, so some convergence may reflect similar inputs.

Why the curve is jagged: changing one token turns an exact duplicate into a unique output. With only 256 outputs, a few such changes visibly move the rate. A downward step therefore need not mean broader recovery from repetitive behaviour.

pages.title: 5. Empirical token entropy
pages.caption: Entropy is calculated from observed token counts in the 16,384-token output probe. The vertical axis is nats, not a percentage.

items.text: Question: is token usage spread across many tokens, or dominated by a small set? Entropy incorporates token frequencies as well as which token types appear.

Behavioural intuition: think of the model's word-use habits. Is it spreading its output across many tokens, or letting a small group dominate? Lower entropy means a more concentrated mix, even if occasional unusual tokens still appear.
Equation: p-hat(t) is token t's observed frequency divided by the total token count. H averages the surprisal -ln p-hat(t). Lower entropy means a more concentrated empirical distribution.
Toy example: two equally frequent tokens have H = ln(2) = 0.693 nats. If one token appears 99% of the time, H is only about 0.056 nats, despite having the same two-token vocabulary.
Difference from distinct-1: distinct-1 counts unique types relative to sample size. Entropy also notices whether a few of those types dominate almost all occurrences.
Our results: Week 1 moves 5.772 -> 5.675. Continued ends at 5.745, close to S0's 5.736. Reset falls to 5.125, showing stronger concentration in token use.

This is observed-output entropy, not the entropy of the model's predicted next-token probabilities. Its exponential is therefore not our real-test perplexity. High entropy can also come from incoherent text; it is not automatically a quality improvement.

Likely causes: the reset arm's later entropy fall is consistent with repeated templates making some tokens disproportionately frequent. Continued training changes the frequency mix differently and ends near S0. Its early rise could reflect a broader or more even mix of tokens, rather than improved understanding.

What remains uncertain: these curves do not identify which token frequencies caused each rise or dip. Similar final entropy can hide different vocabularies and phrase structures, so continued entropy returning near S0 does not establish recovery of the original distribution.

pages.title: 6. Outputs scored by the frozen real-trained model
pages.caption: Week 1 uses frozen G0; Week 2 uses frozen S0. Within each panel the reference weights are held fixed while the generated texts change.

items.text: Question: how predictable are later outputs under the original real-data-trained reference model? Here the model doing the scoring stays fixed, while the text being scored changes.

Behavioural intuition: ask the original real-trained model to read its descendants' writing. Does it find their phrasing familiar or surprising? A higher score means it finds that writing less expected. Very familiar, repetitive phrases can receive a low score without being good answers.
Equation: y is a saved continuation from cycle g. The fixed reference scores targets 2-64 of each of 256 continuations: 16,128 targets. The original prompt is excluded.

Direction: a larger score means the generated continuations are less predictable under the reference; a smaller score means they are more predictable. Neither direction is a stand-alone quality verdict.

Our results: continued rises 1.446 -> 2.343 nats per target. Final reset scores 2.127. Reset output is more predictable under S0 than continued output, while also being more repetitive on several measures.

Reference-score histograms show variation across continuations: rightward means less predictable under the reference. This score is not KL divergence and does not measure factuality or prompt relevance.

Likely causes of the hump: synthetic training initially changes the generated wording, making it less expected under S0. Later concentration on phrases S0 already considers likely could pull the score down. The reset arm's falling late score alongside rising repetition is consistent with this explanation.

Why real-test PPL can still rise: the reference is becoming less surprised by the generated text, while the changing model is becoming more surprised by real text. These are different scoring directions. We have not isolated the cause of the exact mid-run peak.

pages.title: 7. Passage losses, distributions and P95
pages.caption: A: continued S0/S1/S10 real-test block losses, using common bins. B: final reset/continued cumulative losses on the same 4,494 blocks. The Week 1 histogram uses the same definition.

items.text: Question: are all passages getting harder, or are a few difficult ones changing the average?

Behavioural intuition: an average is like a class's average exam mark; it can hide whether everyone struggles or only a few students do. These plots reveal whether prediction worsens broadly. P95 focuses on the difficult end; the median describes a typical passage.
Histogram A: x is block NLL; y is density. Area represents passage fractions. A rightward shift means higher losses.
Cumulative curve B: at a given x-value, height is the percentage of blocks with loss at or below it. Further left generally means lower loss.
Median and P95: the median is the middle block loss. P95 is the 95th percentile: approximately 95% of blocks have loss at or below it. Final P95 is 4.629 for reset versus 4.998 for continued.
Paired result: reset has lower loss on 4,340/4,494 blocks (96.57%); mean NLL is 3.740 versus 4.017, a 0.277-nat difference. The percentage describes passages, not confidence.

Mean passage PPL and SD: exponentiating each block's loss gives difficult passages extra weight before averaging. Continued S10 has corpus PPL 55.56, passage-PPL mean 67.50 and SD 44.79. This SD describes passage variation, not uncertainty across training runs.

Likely causes: a broad rightward shift is consistent with synthetic training changing predictions across many real contexts. Resetting to S0 may preserve more of the real-trained predictions, explaining its leftward advantage over continued training. The matched-block result supports broad deterioration, but does not prove its cause.
Why some passages are harder: unusual names or structures might surprise the model more. We have not annotated these passages; a high block loss does not by itself identify rare-token loss.

pages.title: 8. Epochs, validation and checkpoint selection
pages.caption: Horizontal axes now count epochs within a cycle, not recursive cycles. Stars identify the lowest real-validation-loss checkpoint among epochs 1-5.

items.text: Question: which checkpoint should produce the next dataset, and what happens if synthetic training continues for more epochs? An epoch is one pass over that cycle's training dataset.

Behavioural intuition: more study can improve recall of the practice material while making performance on the real exam worse. Here the practice material is synthetic text and the exam is fixed real text. The star keeps the trained checkpoint that transfers best to that exam.

Selection equation: e-star is the epoch with the smallest fixed real validation NLL. Validation chooses the checkpoint; test data never make that choice. The unmodified starting checkpoint is not among the candidates.
Read the curves: in these cycles real validation loss rises after epoch 1, so the first epoch is selected. Further fitting of synthetic targets can worsen prediction on real text.

Executed versus inherited: continued training executed 50 epochs, but S10 inherits the ten selected synthetic epochs after S0. The reset branch executed 45 new epochs, but A10 starts from S0 and retains its own selected cycle-10 epoch. Its data still carry earlier recursive history.

Training loss, intuitively: how surprising the current practice material is to the model. It measures NLL on training targets, not real-text ability. Different cycles contain different practice material, so their losses also reflect different dataset difficulty.

Fresh optimizer: both Week 2 arms restart AdamW and the learning-rate scheduler every cycle. Continued weights do not mean continued optimizer state. Epoch 1 was selected in every synthetic cycle of the continued and new reset arms.

Observed evidence: in continued cycle 1, training loss falls from 1.112 to 0.889 over epochs 1-5, while real validation loss rises from 3.892 to 4.007. The model fits its synthetic targets better while predicting real text worse.

Likely cause: further updates favour the synthetic distribution at the expense of real-text prediction, consistent with overfitting or distribution mismatch. These curves cannot separate the mechanisms. Selection does not imply epoch 0 was worse; it was not a candidate.

pages.title: 9. Data size, runtime and resource statistics
pages.caption: New work only: Week 1 trains G0-G10; continued imports S0; reset imports S0/S1 and runs A2-A10. Reset hours/debit are rounded report values. Debit includes storage and differing observation windows.

items.text: Question: where did the computation go, and did data size stay constant?

Behavioural intuition: data size is the amount of study material, epochs count rereading it, runtime is the stopwatch and cost is the bill. Throughput is processing speed; peak memory is working space. They help distinguish a behaviour change from simply doing more work.
Equal dataset size: each full dataset has 37,946 x 64 = 2,428,544 input tokens and 37,946 x 63 = 2,390,598 prediction targets per epoch. Prompts are excluded from synthetic training targets.
Fixed evaluation/probe sizes: validation/test score 247,086/283,122 targets. The probe has 16,384 tokens and 15,616 four-gram positions from 256 fixed prompts; it is not a random corpus sample.
Runtime A: bars sum new training/generation durations; diamonds mark provisioning-to-completion time. Gaps include other work and accounting scope.
Epochs B: 55, 50 and 45 new executed epochs. Imported shared stages are not repeated.
Cost C: about $2.23, $3.99 and $3.36 observed account debits, including storage. These are not itemized compute invoices or matched efficiency comparisons.

Speed and memory: throughput is processed training targets or continuations per second. Peak allocated GPU bytes are the process allocator's peak, not all machine VRAM. Forecasts estimate future time from benchmarks.

Why these bars differ: generation must produce tokens successively and maintain five beams, while training can process known token positions in parallel. Imported stages explain the smaller new epoch counts. Week 1 used a cheaper GPU class, so a longer run can still cost less; storage and billing windows also affect debit.

Why sizes and memory are stable: fixed block counts and 64-token lengths enforce equal dataset sizes. The same model and batch settings largely fix memory demand. The last generation is much shorter because it produces only the 256-output probe; forecasts can differ from actual time because of workload and overhead.

pages.title: 10. Reading the measurements together
pages.caption: Same Week 2 reference and final models, viewed through three different measurements. Prediction, phrase reuse and token-frequency spread do not rank the models identically.

items.text: Behavioural intuition: a model can still give real sentences reasonable probabilities while usually choosing a narrow set of favourite phrases when it writes. Better real-text prediction and more repetitive generated answers can therefore coexist.

Observed result: reset A10 has lower PPL than continued B10, but higher four-gram repetition, more exact duplicates and lower entropy. Both final perplexities remain worse than S0; diversity does not change uniformly.

Likely explanation: resetting may preserve the real-trained starting knowledge while recursively generated data still concentrate output. Continued training additionally carries weight changes forward. This is a plausible account of the matched pair, not proof of the mechanism.

Limits: one seeded chain per condition, fixed real prompts, deterministic decoding and real-validation selection. Exact transient peaks and dips remain unresolved; passage variation is not independent-run uncertainty.
